question: Since 2019, almost 2 700 newsstands have closed across Italy (a fall of over 16%), including 2 327 owned by a sole proprietor. These figures are alarming given that Italy’s current total of 11 000 newsstands is dwarfed by its figure of 36 000 twenty years ago.

The ever-increasing decline in sales of printed newspapers and magazines to the benefit of online sales continues to aggravate the risk of the 'desertification' in many municipalities, while at the same time jeopardising the role of newsstands as a channel of information in a community.

According to research in the sector, 25% of Italian municipalities do not have a newsstand, while 30% have only one point of sale for the written press. Given that Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union enshrines the ‘freedom to hold opinions and to communicate information and ideas without interference by public authorities and regardless of frontiers’, can the Commission say: 1.
What it will do to put an end to the current crisis in the sector and combat the resulting social damage?
Whether it agrees that the continuing closures of newsstands pose a risk to the right to information of all those citizens who still use them?
Whether it intends to allocate any funds to protecting newsagents?
answer: While the support to news media is mostly the competence of Member States, the Commission has been keen to help address EU-wide challenges. Besides adopting the Media and Audiovisual Action Plan (1) for the recovery of the media sector, the Commission: —

Is implementing the pilot project ‘Supporting local and regional media in the face of emerging news deserts’ (2). The project produced a mapping of news deserts in Europe and identified practices Member States can adopt in order to cover all communities. It also set up a financing scheme as part of a pilot project, explicitly mentioning as a challenge that ‘existing physical selling points are disappearing’. 42 media projects have been supported, focusing on increasing media pluralism and reaching citizens.

Has been earmarking specific budget from the Creative Europe programme (3) since 2023 to support media of particular relevance to democracy, targeting the ‘improvement of distribution and dissemination of news’. Close to EUR 7 million will be spent on this action in 2024 in order to uphold citizens’ right to access information. The Commission intends to continue financing this priority.

Allows for the reskilling of newsstands workers through the European Social Fund+ which, under this multiannual financial framework, targets lifelong learning and career transitions (EUR 7.7 billion), the adaptation of workers and enterprises (EUR 5.6 billion) and support to active inclusion and employability (EUR 12.9 billion).

Procured a study on the public financing of news media in the EU (4). It mentions practices which Member States take or can take to support newsstands, such as providing support to businesses through direct subsidies or reduced social security contributions.
